structure.title: I. Background and Data - institutional background (workers' compensation and designated doctor process)
I. Background and Data - data and sample, summary statistics (Table 1)
II. Empirical Strategy - estimating equation and balance check (Table 2)
III.A Baseline results from randomized evaluations (Table 3, Figure 1)
III.B Mechanisms and additional evidence, heterogeneity (Tables 4-5, Figure 2)
IV. Broader evidence: gender gap and gender homophily (Tables 6-7)

observations.statement: The paper defines its parameter of interest as the differential effect of being assigned a female rather than male evaluating doctor on female claimants relative to male claimants, isolated through a triple interaction term, and states that once county-by-credential fixed effects are included, claimant characteristics should be unrelated to assigned doctor gender.

The design is framed as exploiting institutional (administrative) conditional random assignment of evaluators to claimants through an automated queue-based process, rather than a researcher-designed experiment, with the authors describing the resulting assignment as isolating as-good-as-random variation in doctor gender.
observations.locator: Section I, Independent Medical Evaluations subsection

observations.statement: The authors discuss a potential threat to the random-assignment argument arising from conflict-of-interest exclusions that are not built into the baseline fixed-effect structure, and address it by pointing to balance results and to alternative specifications with richer fixed effects.

The paper notes an alternative way to isolate conditional random assignment (controlling for injury type by county rather than credential by county) and explains why the chosen approach is preferred, while showing the alternative gives similar estimates in the appendix.

The analysis sample is built by linking several administrative sources obtained through open records requests, including exam records, cash and medical benefit files, and doctor-gender information from a national provider registry supplemented with state licensing board files.
observations.locator: Section I, Data and Sample subsection

observations.statement: The baseline sample is restricted to designated-doctor evaluations for injuries occurring after the automated (rather than manually assigned) doctor-assignment system was implemented, with outcomes measured over a fixed post-exam follow-up window and an exam-year cutoff chosen so follow-up data are available for every claim.
observations.locator: Section I, Data and Sample subsection

observations.statement: Claimants with missing gender information are dropped, and exams requiring a designated doctor with a specific board-certified sub-specialty are excluded because such assignments would not be governed by the general credential-by-county random-assignment rule the design relies on.
observations.locator: Section I, footnote 16 and Data and Sample subsection

observations.statement: Different analyses draw on different nested samples: exams with an independent medical evaluation for the baseline gender-match analysis, the full universe of claims for the broader gender-gap analysis, and claims with an identifiable treating doctor for the homophily analysis, with each table's notes stating which sample and its size.

The unit of observation for the baseline analysis is a single independent medical exam (effectively one claimant's first designated-doctor evaluation), and the paper explains that it focuses on the first evaluation because later evaluations for the same claim are not exogenously assigned.
observations.locator: Section I, Data and Sample subsection

observations.statement: Two primary outcomes are constructed: a binary indicator for receiving any additional cash benefits after the exam, and a normalized measure of additional cash benefits that revalues benefits at a population-wide average benefit rate so the measure is not mechanically driven by an individual's own pre-injury earnings.
observations.locator: Section I, Data and Sample subsection

observations.statement: The key explanatory variables are indicators for the assigned doctor being female and for the claimant being female, with the object of interest constructed as their interaction rather than either indicator alone.

Several balance and control variables are entered in logs, including measures of medical spending and weeks between injury and exam, when used as dependent variables in the balance checks or as controls.
All monetary variables are converted to a common price-year basis using a consumer price index series before being used in the analysis.
observations.locator: Section I, Data and Sample subsection

observations.statement: One claimant characteristic used in a supplemental table is a predicted-benefits variable built from a machine-learning (lasso) model rather than observed directly, and the authors note that some baseline variables like pre-injury wage are only available for a subset of claims and can be influenced by the exam outcome itself.
observations.locator: Section I footnote 18 and Section III footnote 28

observations.statement: The baseline fixed effects (county-by-credential, exam year, injury year) are described in the surrounding text and table notes rather than shown as rows in the main results table, while only the additional doctor fixed effect is shown as an explicit indicator row.

The broader gender-gap table adds controls in successive columns, moving from no controls through insurer, injury timing, geography, age and diagnosis fixed effects to a fully saturated specification, so readers can see how the estimated gap moves as controls accumulate.

Every main results table reports the regression sample size, and different tables report different sample sizes corresponding to the exam-level, full-claims, or treating-doctor-choice samples used in that analysis.

Results tables report the mean of the dependent variable, and for the baseline gender-match table also report the mean of the dependent variable specifically among female claimants evaluated by male doctors, to give readers a benchmark for interpreting the estimated effect sizes.

Table notes throughout the paper explicitly state the level at which standard errors are clustered, and report p-values in brackets beneath each coefficient in addition to standard errors in parentheses.

The main results table presents a baseline specification in the first columns of each outcome block, followed immediately by variant columns that add a doctor fixed effect or restrict the sample to female claimants only, within the same table.

The broader gender-gap and homophily tables list each fixed-effect or control block as a labeled row with an 'x' marking which columns include it, making the progression of controls across columns explicit.

Standard errors in the baseline analysis are clustered at the evaluating-doctor level, with the stated rationale that residuals in a given doctor's exam decisions may be correlated with each other across that doctor's exams.

The paper states that its clustering choice is checked against alternative clustering levels and against unclustered standard errors, with these comparisons relegated to the online appendix rather than shown in the main tables.

A dedicated balance table regresses predetermined claimant and injury characteristics on the doctor-gender and interaction terms from the baseline specification, checking that assignment is unrelated to characteristics that should not be affected by which doctor a claimant draws.

Beyond formal balance checks, the paper runs a falsification-style exercise interacting doctor gender with a range of other claimant characteristics, and separately interacting claimant gender with a range of other doctor characteristics, to see whether the documented pattern is really about gender rather than a correlated characteristic.
observations.note: Framed by the authors as a robustness/mechanism check rather than a named diagnostic, but functions like a placebo-characteristic test.

observations.statement: A more granular version of the subgroup heterogeneity check, broken out by finer injury-type categories, is reported only in the online appendix rather than in the main text.
observations.locator: Section III.B text referencing online Appendix Figure A1

observations.statement: Robustness to richer fixed-effect structures, including interactions of the baseline county-by-credential fixed effect with exam year or exam quarter, is presented in the online appendix to address possible changes over time in the pool of available doctors within a county.
observations.locator: Section I footnote 15 and Section III.A closing paragraph

observations.statement: The paper reports that similar implied percentage effects are obtained from an alternative linear specification for the benefits outcome and from a specification using unadjusted benefits while controlling directly for pre-injury wage, both shown only in the online appendix.

Within the main results table itself, the paper shows the baseline estimate is similar when a doctor fixed effect is added and when the sample is restricted to female claimants only, rather than deferring these checks entirely to an appendix.

Robustness to progressively adding baseline claimant and injury controls to the main specification is summarized in a pair of online appendix tables, which the text describes as showing stable coefficients as controls are added.
observations.locator: Section III.B, Magnitude Relative to Gender Gap subsection

observations.statement: Heterogeneity in the female-doctor by female-claimant interaction is examined by splitting the sample along demographic, injury-severity, industry and prior-experience characteristics, with the stated purpose of using these patterns to shed light on possible mechanisms rather than to establish a policy-relevant subgroup result.
observations.locator: Section III.B, Heterogeneity Analyses subsection and Figure 2

observations.statement: A separate set of regressions interacts the female-doctor indicator with other observed doctor characteristics (credential type, medical-school ranking, specialty, experience) to test whether gender differences in evaluation load onto these correlated doctor traits instead of gender itself.

Effect sizes for both outcomes are expressed as percentage-point and percent changes relative to the mean outcome level among female claimants evaluated by male doctors, giving a natural benchmark group for interpreting the magnitude.

The discussion section translates the estimated effects into back-of-envelope counterfactual policy exercises, such as how much of the observed conditional gender gap would close under a hypothetical shift in the gender composition of evaluators or in the degree of gender-matched assignment.

The introduction situates the paper's motivating gender gap against a comparable finding from prior research on disability-insurance denial rates by gender, positioning the Texas workers'-compensation setting within a broader pattern documented elsewhere.

Key point estimates are consistently accompanied by explicit statements of their confidence intervals in the running text, not just in table notes, when the paper discusses the size of the baseline effects.
observations.locator: Section III.A discussion of Table 3 and Figure 1

observations.statement: The authors explicitly state that their design cannot conceptually or empirically distinguish among candidate mechanisms for the gender-match effect, such as provider discrimination versus differences in how patients communicate with own-gender doctors.

The paper cautions that appropriate care should be taken in extrapolating estimates from the disputed-claims sample with independent medical evaluations to the broader population of workers'-compensation claimants, even though gender patterns look similar across the two populations.

The authors note there is no objective benchmark for the correct level of evaluated disability or efficient benefit generosity, so the results cannot establish whether female doctors are too lenient or male doctors are too strict, only that the two groups evaluate differently.
Subgroup heterogeneity results are displayed as a coefficient plot with capped horizontal bars for confidence intervals across many subgroup definitions, rather than as a large table of coefficients.
Every regression table's notes state which sample the estimates are drawn from, which controls and fixed effects are included, and the clustering level of reported standard errors.

Supplementary tables and figures are consistently labeled with an 'A' prefix and referenced by number throughout the main text (for example as alternative-specification or alternative fixed-effect checks), though these online appendix items are not part of the supplied text.
observations.locator: Multiple footnotes referencing online Appendix Tables/Figures

observations.statement: A dedicated summary statistics table compares claimant characteristics across the full claims population and the randomized-evaluation subsample, and separately compares designated doctors to broader populations of doctors treating workers'-compensation patients, all Texas doctors, and all US doctors.
The paper reports exact p-values in brackets beneath each coefficient rather than using significance-star notation in its regression tables.
The introduction previews the direction and relative size of the main gender-match findings for female versus male claimants before the reader reaches the empirical strategy or results sections.

Near the end of the introduction the paper contains an explicit paragraph enumerating the several literatures it contributes to (health disparities, doctor-patient race or gender match, and authority-figure gender effects), functioning as a contribution statement.

The paper presents institutional background and data construction as a full section before introducing the estimating equation, so the empirical strategy section follows rather than precedes the data description.

Mechanism-oriented analysis (other-characteristic placebo checks and subgroup heterogeneity) is presented as a subsection immediately following the baseline results, before the paper moves on to broader-population evidence and survey evidence.

The paper relies heavily on an online appendix for many robustness checks, an alternative fixed-effect specification, a finer heterogeneity breakdown, and additional survey tables, with the main text repeatedly pointing readers to appendix tables and sections rather than reproducing them.
observations.locator: Throughout, e.g. footnotes 15, 17, 22, 25 and Section V footnotes
observations.note: Inferred from the frequency of online-appendix references across sections; the appendix itself is not part of the supplied text (online_appendix_not_available).

observations.statement: The authors explicitly label their evidence on whether male doctors apply a stricter standard to female patients (from the controls-augmented specification) as only suggestive, not conclusive, given the lack of an objective disability benchmark.
observations.locator: Section III.B, Magnitude Relative to Gender Gap subsection

observations.statement: A supplemental survey of adults with recent work experience is used as external, non-administrative evidence to explore why gender match might matter, asking about past negative experiences with providers and expectations about own-gender versus opposite-gender doctors.

The paper discusses how its findings, based on one state's disputed workers'-compensation claims, might scale to broader policy contexts, including a separate back-of-envelope extrapolation exercise for the full (non-disputed) claims population using different data and assumptions.
observations.locator: Section IV introduction and Section VI, Discussion

observations.statement: A formal replication-data citation for the paper, deposited with a data-archiving distributor and assigned its own DOI, appears in the reference list, though no separate data-availability statement section or explicit code-availability language is present in the extracted text.

The core dataset is assembled from state-agency administrative records obtained through open records requests rather than purchased commercial data or a public-use survey, and is merged with a federal provider registry and state licensing-board files.
observations.locator: Section I, Data and Sample subsection

observations.statement: In addition to administrative data, the paper collects new primary data through a commissioned online survey platform, with eligibility criteria set to approximate the working-age population at risk of a workplace injury.

gaps: No explicit multiple-testing correction is stated despite many characteristic-interaction and subgroup comparisons (Tables 4 and 5, Figure 2).
No preregistration or pre-analysis plan is mentioned for either the administrative-data analysis or the supplemental survey.
No IRB approval, ethics approval, or participant consent language appears anywhere in the extracted text for the survey.
No statistical software or package (e.g., Stata, R, Python) is named anywhere in the main text.
No dedicated 'Data Availability Statement' section appears in the extracted text; the only replication reference is a data citation in the reference list.
No sample weights are mentioned for any reported regression.
Online appendix content (referenced repeatedly as online Appendix Tables/Figures A1-A10 and Sections A-D) is a separate document and is not part of the supplied extracted text.

reading.note: Read the complete extracted text: title, abstract, all seven numbered sections (Background and Data; Empirical Strategy; Differences in Evaluations by Doctor Gender; Broader Evidence; Survey Evidence; Discussion; Conclusion) and the reference list, pages 1-38. No appendix pages are included in this text; the online appendix referenced throughout (Tables/Figures A1-A10, Sections A-D) is a separate document not supplied for this note.
